heroHeadline: Moody's Strips US of Last Aaa Rating — First Time ALL THREE Agencies Below Top Grade; 30Y Treasury Briefly Tops 5.00%; Warsh-Powell June FOMC Showdown Risk Emerges on Day 4
heroSubtitle: On Monday May 18, 2026 — Day 4 of Kevin Warsh's Federal Reserve chairmanship — markets absorbed the historic Moody's Aa1 downgrade announced after markets closed Friday. For the first time since Moody's assigned the US a Aaa rating in 1917, all three major credit rating agencies (S&P in 2011, Fitch in 2023, and now Moody's) have simultaneously downgraded the United States below their respective top ratings. Moody's cited a federal deficit projected at approximately 9% of GDP by 2034 — up from 6.4% — and debt-to-GDP reaching 134% by 2035, with successive administrations and Congresses failing to reverse the structural deterioration. The Monday market reaction was significant: the 30-year Treasury yield briefly surpassed 5.00% for the first time since late 2023, the S&P 500 closed at 7,382.65 (-0.35%), the Nasdaq at 26,054.08 (-0.65%), and the Russell 2000 fell 2.44% as small-cap leverage sensitivity to rising long yields dominated. The Moody's downgrade compounds the tightening dynamic already set in motion by Warsh's plans to aggressively reduce the $6.7 trillion Fed balance sheet ('blow up the playbook'), since QT-driven Treasury selling and downgrade-driven reduced demand for Treasuries push in the same yield-rising direction. Analysts flagged a Warsh-Powell showdown risk at the June 16-17 FOMC: Powell remains on the Board of Governors until January 2028 with opposing policy views, April already saw four dissents (most since 1992), and the Fed's May inflation forecast is described as 'ugly.' Recession probabilities stand at Goldman Sachs 30%, JPMorgan 35%, and Moody's Analytics 49%, with Bank of America forecasting no rate cuts until July 2027. The week ahead includes April housing starts (May 21) and Flash PMIs (May 22).
